o:
The operation nums[i] := nums[i] AND (nums[i] XOR x) can only CLEAR bits of nums[i]: for any bit set in nums[i], choosing x's bit appropriately turns it off; bits not in nums[i] stay off. Bits can never be created. Crucially, each bit position is independent across the array — we can clear bits of different elements separately.

So bit b can appear in the final XOR iff at least one element has bit b set (keep it there, clear conflicting contributions elsewhere if needed). Hence the answer is simply the bitwise OR of all elements.

Example 1: 3|2|4|6 = 7 ✓. Example 2: 1|2|3|9|2 = 11 ✓ (achieved with zero operations).
k: The operation only clears bits within a single element; it never sets new bits.
Bit positions are independent: bit b is achievable iff some element contains bit b.
Therefore the maximum XOR equals the OR of all elements.

a.n: Approach 1: Bitwise OR of All Elements
a.i: Fold OR over the array. Each set bit in the OR comes from some element and can be preserved (clear other elements' copies of that bit if parity demands), and no absent bit can ever appear.
s: OR every element into the answer.
a.t: O(n) — a single fold over the array.

w: The whole problem is recognizing the clearing-only nature of `a AND (a XOR x)`. Common wrong guess: XOR of all elements (that's merely one achievable value, sometimes optimal by luck). Follow-up: if the operation could also SET bits, the answer would be unbounded/all-ones; discuss how the constraint shapes reachability.
